Abhidharmakośabhāṣyam, First Chapter on Elements. Oṃ, homage to the Buddha!

Having paid homage to Him who has utterly destroyed all darkness in every respect and who has lifted the world out of the mire of cyclic existence—that Teacher of reality as it is—I shall proclaim the treatise known as the Abhidharmakośa. (1)
Desiring to compose this treatise, he begins with a salutation to his Teacher, preceded by a description of his qualities, in order to make known the greatness of that Teacher.
The word "ya" refers to the Buddha, the Blessed One. He is called "one who has destroyed darkness" (hatāndhakāra) because darkness has been destroyed by him or because he has destroyed it.
Since he has destroyed darkness in every way and regarding everything, he is "one who has completely and entirely destroyed all darkness" (sarvathā-sarva-hatāndhakāra).
Ignorance is indeed darkness because it obstructs the vision of reality.

And that [ignorance] has been destroyed in the Blessed Buddha by the attainment of its antidote—being, in every way, everywhere, and for all objects of knowledge, subject to the nature of non-arising.
Therefore, he is one who has destroyed darkness in every respect and in its entirety.
Even Pratyekabuddhas and Śrāvakas have indeed destroyed the darkness regarding all [objects], due to the absolute departure of afflicted delusion;
yet not in every respect.
For indeed, regarding these qualities of a Buddha—objects that are extremely remote in space and time, and which possess infinite varieties—there exists a non-afflicted ignorance.

Having praised the Blessed One for his perfection in the practice for his own benefit, he now praises that same Blessed One for his perfection in the practice for the benefit of others, saying: "He has lifted the world out of the mire of saṃsāra.
For saṃsāra is like a mire, because it is a place where the world is stuck and because it is difficult to cross.
The Blessed One, feeling compassion for the world submerged therein and without protection, has uplifted it according to their capacity by extending the hand of the teaching of the True Dharma.
Having paid homage to him who is thus endowed with the perfection of practice for the benefit of himself and others— having prostrated with the head—
the term "Teacher of Reality" (*yathārthaśāstā*) refers to one who teaches in accordance with reality, that is, without error.
By this, he reveals the means for his practice of benefiting others:
being a Teacher because he teaches according to reality, he has pulled the world out from the mire of saṃsāra,
and not by the power of supernatural feats or the granting of boons.
Having paid homage to him, he states what he will do: "I shall expound the treatise" (*śāstra*).
It is called a *śāstra* because it instructs (*śāsana*) the disciples.
Which treatise? He says: "The Abhidharmakośa."
What is this so-called Abhidharma? Abhidharma is stainless wisdom along with its attendants. In this context, wisdom is the discernment of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*).
"Pure" means untainted (*anāsrava*).
"With its attendants" means with its retinue.
Thus, it is stated that Abhidharma consists of the five untainted aggregates (*pañcaskandhaka*).
This, then, is the ultimate Abhidharma.
The conventional [path], however, consists of whatever teaching and whatever treatise lead to its attainment;

it also includes the contaminated wisdom (*sāsravā prajñā*) consisting of hearing, reflection, and cultivation, as well as that acquired at birth (*upapattipratilambhikā*), together with their attendants;
and it includes the treatises for the sake of attaining this uncontaminated wisdom (*anāsravā prajñā*).
That too is called Abhidharma because it serves as the equipment (*sambhāra*) for that [Abhidharma].
As for the etymological definition (*nirvacana*): it is "Dharma" because it maintains its own characteristic (*svalakṣaṇadhāraṇāt*).
Thus, this is "Abhidharma" because it is a Dharma that is directed toward (*abhimukha*) either the ultimate Dharma, which is Nirvāṇa, or the characteristic of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*).
The Abhidharma has been explained.
But how is this treatise the *Abhidharmakośa*?
Because its meaning is fully contained within this [treatise], or because it is the basis for that [Abhidharma], it is called the *Abhidharmakośa*. (2)
For that Abhidharma, known as the treatise (*śāstra*), is included within this [work] according to its primary meaning; thus, this treatise serves as its sheath (*kośa*).
Alternatively, that Abhidharma is the basis (*āśraya*) of this treatise, for it has been extracted from that.
Therefore, since that very [Abhidharma] is the treasury (kośa) of this [treatise], this work is called the *Abhidharmakośa*.
But for what purpose is the instruction of Abhidharma, and by whom was it first taught, such that the Master takes care to speak the *Abhidharmakośa*?
He says: Because apart from the discernment (*pravicaya*) of phenomena (*dharmas*), there is no means for the pacification of the afflictions (*kleśas*).
And it is because of the afflictions that the world wanders here in this ocean of existence; for that reason, it is said, this [treatise] was uttered by the Teacher. //3//

Since there is no means for the pacification of the afflictions (*kleśa*) apart from the discernment of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*), and since it is the afflictions that cause the world to wander in this great ocean of *saṃsāra*,
it is for that reason— and for the sake of that discernment of phenomena— that the Teacher, the Buddha, is said to have taught the Abhidharma.
For without the instruction of the Abhidharma, a disciple is not capable of discerning phenomena.

The Vaibhāṣikas say: "That [Abhidharma], however, was taught by the Blessed One in a scattered manner; it was then compiled and established by the Venerable Kātyāyanīputra and others, just as the Venerable Dharmatrāta composed the Udānavarga."
Furthermore, what are those phenomena for the sake of which the instruction of Abhidharma is intended? He says:
"Phenomena are either with outflows (sāsrava) or without outflows (anāsrava).
This is the concise exposition of all phenomena."
In that regard, what are the contaminated phenomena? It is said: conditioned phenomena, excluding the Path, are contaminated.
With the exception of the truth of the path, all other conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are with outflows (*sāsrava*).
What is the reason?
Because the outflows (*āsrava*) adhere to them. (Verse 4)
Granted that outflows (āsrava) may arise even with the truths of cessation and the path as their objects, they do not adhere (anuśerate) therein;
thus, there is no consequence of those two being "with outflows" (sāsrava).
How they do not adhere will be explained later, precisely in the exposition of the underlying tendencies (anuśaya).
The contaminated [dharmas] have been explained.
What are the untainted (anāsrava) phenomena? The untainted are the truth of the path and the threefold unconditioned (asaṃskṛta). What are the threefold [unconditioned]?
Space and the two types of cessation.
Which two?
Cessation through deliberation and cessation not through deliberation.
Thus, these three kinds of unconditioned phenomena—space and so forth—and the truth of the path are the untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas.
For what reason?
Because the outflows (*āsrava*) do not adhere (*anuśerate*) within them.
Regarding these three kinds of unconditioned phenomena that have been mentioned, among them, space is non-obstruction. (5)
Space has the nature of non-obstruction, wherein matter moves.
Cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*) is that which is dissociation.
That dissociation from contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) is cessation through deliberation.

Deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā*) is the discernment of the Noble Truths, such as suffering; it is a specific kind of wisdom (*prajñā*). Cessation attained by means of that [wisdom] is cessation through deliberation.
This is due to the elision of the middle term, as in the case of "ox-cart" (*goratha*).
But is there only one analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*) for all contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena?
He says: "No."
Rather, they are distinct.
For as many as there are substances of conjunction, so many are there substances of disjunction.
Otherwise, it would follow that by realizing the cessation of the afflictions to be abandoned through the vision of suffering, one would realize the cessation of all afflictions.
If this were the case, the cultivation of the remaining antidotes would be rendered useless.
As for what was stated, "Cessation is without a counterpart (asabhāga)," what is its meaning?
The meaning of this statement is that it has no homogeneous cause (sabhāgahetu), nor does it belong to anything; it does not mean that there is nothing similar to it.
Cessation through deliberation has been explained.
The other cessation, which is the absolute obstruction of arising, is [attained] through non-analytical means. //6//
The cessation that is other than disjunction—which acts as an absolute obstacle to the arising of future dharmas—is non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
For this is not obtained through analytical discernment;
rather, it is obtained through the deficiency of conditions.

For example, when the eye and mind are occupied with a single form, other forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles pass by; it is impossible for the five groups of consciousness (*vijñānakāya*) that have those [other objects] as their objects to arise again.
For they lack the capacity to take a past object as their objective support.
Therefore, their non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*) is attained due to the deficiency of conditions.
And in this regard, there is a fourfold alternative (catuṣkoṭika):
there are those dharmas for which only analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyānirodha) is obtained;
namely, the contaminated (sāsrava) dharmas that are past, present, or destined to arise.

There are those for whom there is only non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*), such as unconditioned phenomena that are untainted (*anāsrava*) and subject to non-arising (*anutpattidharma*). There are those for whom both exist.
For example, there are those that are outflow-tainted and have the nature of non-arising;
there are those for which neither [of these two] exists;
and there are those that are untainted and have the nature of having arisen in the past or present.
The three kinds of unconditioned phenomena have been explained.
As for what was stated, "Conditioned phenomena, excluding the Path,
are with-outflows (sāsrava)," which are those conditioned phenomena?
Those conditioned phenomena, moreover, are the five aggregates beginning with form (rūpa).
The aggregate of form, the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of mental formations, and the aggregate of consciousness are conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*).
Since there exists something that has been produced,
there is no contradiction regarding future things because they belong to that same class, just as in the case of milk.
These very [factors] are the time-periods (adhvan), the bases of discourse (kathāvastu), those with departure (saniḥsāra), and those with a basis (savastuka). //7//
The paths (adhvan) are so called because they consist of that which has gone, is going, and will go;
or alternatively, because they are consumed by impermanence.
Discourse (kathā) is speech.
Its basis is "name" (nāman).
However, because it grasps a basis that possesses meaning, the conditioned is called the "basis of discourse" (kathāvastu);
otherwise, the *Prakaraṇapāda* treatise would be contradicted by the statement: "The bases of discourse are subsumed within the eighteen elements (dhātu)."
The escape (*niḥsaraṇa*) and the core-essence (*niḥsāra*) of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) is nirvāṇa.
Because they possess this [nirvāṇa], they are "with escape" (*saniḥsāra*).
Because they have causes, they are "with a basis" (*savastuka*).
The Vaibhāṣikas maintain that the word "entity" (vastu) indeed signifies a cause (hetu).
These are the synonyms for conditioned phenomena.
Furthermore, those very conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) which are with outflows (*sāsrava*) are the aggregates of clinging (*upādānaskandha*).
What is established by this?
That which is an aggregate of clinging is also an aggregate (*skandha*).
There may be aggregates (skandhas) that are not aggregates of clinging (upādānaskandhas),
namely, untainted (anāsrava) conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra).
In this context, "clinging" (upādāna) refers to the afflictions (kleśas).
They are called "appropriation-aggregates" (*upādāna-skandha*) because they arise from appropriation, like a fire from grass or chaff;
or because they are subject to it, like a king's servant;
or because appropriation arises from them, like flowers and fruits from a tree.
Those very same contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena are also called "with conflict" (*saraṇa*).

For the afflictions (*kleśa*) are indeed "conflicts" (*raṇa*), because they cause harm to oneself and others; and because those [phenomena] are underlain by them (*anuśayitatva*), they are "with conflict."
Like that which is with outflows (*sāsrava*), they are suffering (*duḥkha*), origin (*samudaya*), the world (*loka*), the basis of views (*dṛṣṭisthāna*), and existence (*bhava*). //8//
It is "suffering" because it is disagreeable to the noble ones;
it is "origination" because suffering arises from it—
thus is the world.
Because a view dwells within this by way of latent proclivity (*anuśayana*), it is called a "basis for views" (*dṛṣṭisthāna*).
It is called "existence" (*bhava*) because it comes to be (*bhavati*).
These are synonymous terms corresponding to the actual meaning of contaminated phenomena (*sāsravadharma*).
It has been stated that there are five aggregates, beginning with form (*rūpa*).
Among these, form consists of the five sense faculties, the five objects, and non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) alone.
The five sense faculties are the faculties of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body.
The five objects are the five respective domains of those very sense-faculties, such as the eye and so forth, known as visible forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles;
and also non-informative matter (*avijñapti*).
Such is the extent of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).

In that regard, those which have been mentioned as the five objects, beginning with visible form, are the translucent forms—the eye and so forth—which serve as the bases for their respective cognitions. (9)

Those five translucent material entities (*rūpaprasāda*) which serve as the bases for the consciousnesses of visible form, sound, odor, taste, and tangible objects should be understood, respectively, as the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body.
As stated by the Blessed One: "O monk, the eye is an internal sense-field (*āyatana*), a translucent materiality derived from the four great elements," and so forth.

Alternatively, those which were mentioned as the eye and so forth are the eye and other [faculties], which are translucent matter (*rūpaprasāda*) serving as the bases for their respective consciousnesses.
The meaning is that they are the bases for visual consciousness and the others.
And by doing so, the *Prakaraṇapāda* treatise is also followed:
"What is the eye?
It is the translucent matter that is the basis of visual consciousness," and so forth.
The five faculties have been explained.
Five objects are to be explained;
among them, first, matter (rūpa) is twofold: color (varṇa) and shape (saṃsthāna).
In that regard, color is of four kinds, beginning with blue;
the others are its subdivisions. Shape is of eight kinds, from long to uneven.
That same sphere of visible form (*rūpāyatana*) is further said to be of twenty kinds, namely:
blue, yellow, red, white, long, short, square, round, high, low, even, uneven, cloud, smoke, dust, mist, shadow, glare, light, and darkness.
Some recite twenty-one kinds, adding "the sky" as a single color.
In that context, "level" refers to even ground;
"uneven" refers to rugged ground;
and "mahikā" refers to mist.
Heat is the radiance of the sun;
light is the radiance of the moon, stars, fire, medicinal herbs, and gems;
shadow is that wherein forms are visible.
From the opposite [of these], there is darkness.
The remainder is not elaborated upon because it is easy to understand.
There is a sphere of visible form that exists by way of color but not by way of shape;
it is what is called blue, yellow, red, white, shadow, glare, light, and darkness.
There is [visible form] that exists by way of shape but not by way of color.
The portion of [the category of] long and so forth that has the nature of bodily intimation exists in both ways;
the remainder is the sense-sphere of visible form.
Others maintain that only heat and light exist as color (varṇa),
for the delimitation of length and so forth is seen in blue and other colors.
But how can a single substance exist in two ways?
Because both [the agent and the object] are perceived therein;
for this root *vid* has the sense of "knowing" (*jñāna*), not the sense of "existence" (*sattā*).
In that case, however, the same consequence would apply even to bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*).
The sense-sphere of form has been explained.
Sound, however, is of eight kinds.
It is first fourfold, being caused by the primary elements (mahābhūta) that are either appropriated or non-appropriated, and being designated as pertaining to sentient beings or non-sentient things.
This, moreover, becomes eightfold through the distinction between the agreeable and the disagreeable.
Among these, that which has appropriated primary elements as its cause is, for example, the sound of the hand or the voice.
That which has non-appropriated primary elements as its cause is, for example, the sound of wind, forest trees, or a river.
That which is designated as a sentient being is the sound of vocal intimation.
Another [type of sound] is called non-sentient (*asattvākhya*).
Others maintain that there is also sound caused by both appropriated (*upātta*) and unappropriated (*anupātta*) primary elements (*mahābhūta*),
such as that produced by the conjunction of a hand and a drum.
But just as a single atom of color is not held to be derived from two sets of the four primary elements, so too it should not be so held in this case.
Sound has been explained.
Taste is sixfold,
distinguished as sweet, sour, salty, pungent, bitter, and astringent.
Odor is fourfold, because pleasant and unpleasant odors are each either balanced or unbalanced.
However, in the treatise it is said to be threefold: "pleasant odor, unpleasant odor, and balanced odor."
The tangible consists of eleven types. // 10 //
The tangible has the nature of eleven substances:
the four great elements, smoothness, roughness, heaviness, lightness, cold, hunger, and thirst.
Among these, we shall explain the primary elements later.
Smoothness is softness;
roughness is harshness;
heaviness is that by which objects are weighed.
Lightness is the opposite [of heaviness].
Coldness is that which produces a desire for warmth. Hunger is that which produces a desire for food.
Thirst is that which produces the desire for drink;
this is a case of applying the name of the effect to the cause.
As it is said: "The arising of Buddhas is blissful; the teaching of the Dharma is blissful."
Harmony in the Saṅgha is happiness; for those who are united, austerity is happiness.
Thus it is said.
In that realm, the realm of form (rūpadhātu), hunger and thirst do not exist;
the remainder exists.
Although garments are not weighed there one by one, they are weighed when accumulated;
cold is not harmful there,
for it is said that it is actually beneficial.

Regarding this manifold form that has been described, visual consciousness sometimes arises from a single substance when there is a discernment of its specific type; sometimes it arises from many substances when there is no such discernment.
This is as, for example, when one sees from a distance an array of troops with various colors and shapes, or a collection of jewels.
In the same way, auditory consciousness and the others are to be understood.
However, some maintain that body-consciousness arises from at most five types of tangibles:
the four great elements and one [quality] such as smoothness.
Others say that [the fruit] is attained by all eleven [faculties].

But if this is so, since they have a composite object, would it not follow that the five groups of consciousness have universals as their objects, rather than particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*)? These are held to have particular characteristics as their objects with respect to the particular characteristic of the sense-field (*āyatana-svalakṣaṇa*), and not with respect to the particular characteristic of the substance (*dravya-svalakṣaṇa*); thus there is no fault. This is now investigated: The five groups of consciousness have the sense-fields as their objects; therefore, they are said to have particular characteristics as their objects. However, the sense-field is a collection of many substances. Consequently, the five groups of consciousness take a composite thing as their object, and thus they do not have particular characteristics as their objects. If one asks how this can be so, [the answer is: these are said to have particular characteristics as their objects because they arise in dependence upon the particular characteristic of the sense-field, and not because they arise in dependence upon the particular characteristic of the substance. For example, when the eye-consciousness arises in dependence upon the particular characteristic of the visual faculty and visible form, it is said to have the particular characteristic as its object because it takes the sense-field as its object. It does not, however, take the particular characteristic of the substance as its object, because it does not apprehend the individual atoms. Therefore, there is no contradiction. Furthermore, the Sūtra states: "The eye-consciousness arises depending on the eye and forms. It does not say that it arises depending on the atoms. Thus, it is established that the five groups of consciousness have the sense-fields as their objects and have particular characteristics as their objects. When the objects of the body and tongue faculties are reached simultaneously, which consciousness arises first? That whose object is more intense [arises first]. However, when the objects are equally reached, the tongue-consciousness arises first, because the mental continuum is dominated by the desire to eat.
The five objects of the sense-faculties have been explained, as well as the manner of their apprehension.
Now, non-informative action (avijñapti) must be explained; it is described as follows:

"That serial continuity, whether wholesome or unwholesome, which exists even in one whose mind is distracted or who is without mind, and which is derived from the primary elements (mahābhūta), is called non-informative action. (11)
"Of one whose mind is distracted" means even of one whose mind is other than that [specific state].
"Even of one who is without mind" means even of one who has entered the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) or the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).
By the word "even," it is understood that this also applies to one whose mind is not distracted and who possesses a mind.
"That which is a continuous succession" (*anubandha*) refers to a stream (*pravāha*).
"Pure and impure" (*śubhāśubha*) refers to wholesome and unwholesome (*kuśalākuśala*).
Since such a stream also exists for acquisitions (*prāpti*), it is stated "derived from the great elements" (*mahābhūtāny upādāya*) in order to distinguish that [stream of matter].
The Vaibhāṣikas maintain that the meaning of "derived" (upādāya) is the meaning of "cause" (hetu),
because it serves as the cause for its arising and so forth.
The word "for" (hi) in the phrase "for that is non-informative" (sa hy avijñaptiḥ) is intended to make known the reason for that designation.
Although its intrinsic nature consists of form and action, it is called "non-informative" (*avijñapti*) because, unlike informative action (*vijñapti*), it does not communicate anything to another.
This indicates the statement of the Master [Vasubandhu].
In brief, however, non-informative action is wholesome or unwholesome form produced by informative action or meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Regarding the phrase “derived from the great elements” (k. 11c), what are these elements? They are the earth element, the water, fire, and wind elements.

These four are called "elements" because they sustain their own specific characteristics and derived matter; they are called the "four great elements" because of their magnitude, which arises from their being the basis for all other forms of matter and their relative coarseness.
Alternatively, it is because these [elements] possess a vast configuration within the aggregates of earth, water, fire, and air when their activities have become manifest.
Furthermore, in what function are these elements established, and what is their intrinsic nature? To this he says:
they are established through functions such as supporting and so forth.
These elements—earth, water, fire, and air—are established respectively in the functions of supporting, cohering, maturing, and expanding.
Furthermore, expansion should be understood as growth and spreading;
this is their function.
Their intrinsic natures, however, are respectively solidity, moisture, heat, and motion. (12)
Hardness is the earth element;
moisture is the water element;
heat is the fire element.
Motion is the wind element (*vāyudhātu*).
It is called "motion" because by means of it the stream of primary elements (*bhūtasrotas*) is moved, being produced in successive locations like the movement of a flame.
"What is the wind element? It is lightness and mobility," as it is taught in the *Prakaraṇapāda* and in the *Sūtra*.
Furthermore, lightness is also stated in the treatises (*prakaraṇa*) to be a derived form (*upādāyarūpa*).
Therefore, that phenomenon whose intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is motion is the wind element (*vāyudhātu*); thus, its intrinsic nature is made manifest through its function (*karman*).
What, then, is the distinction between earth and so forth, and the earth-element and so forth?
Earth is designated by worldly convention as color and shape;
for when people point out earth, they point out its color and its shape.
Just as with earth, so it is with water and fire;
only color and shape are spoken of by worldly convention,
whereas wind is indeed the element itself.
That which is indeed the wind element is what is called "wind" in the world; and yet, moreover: //13//
Just as the earth is spoken of by worldly convention as "color" and "shape," so too is the wind:
[one speaks of] a blue whirlwind or a circular whirlwind.
Why, then, is this aggregate of form (rūpaskandha), ending with the unmanifest (avijñapti), so called? Because of being affected (rūpaṇāt).
It was said by the Blessed One: "It is affected, O monks, it is affected; therefore it is called the appropriated aggregate of form."
"By what is it affected?
Even when touched by the touch of a hand, it is affected. This is the full explanation.
"Is affected" means it is oppressed.
For it is said in the *Arthavargīya*: "If those desires do not come to fruition for that embodied being who yearns for them and is born of longing, he suffers as if pierced by an arrow.
But what, then, is the affliction regarding form?

Others say that "matter" (rūpa) consists in transformation, production, resistance, and deformation. In that case, however, the matter of an atom would not qualify as matter, because it lacks deformation.

Indeed, a single atom does not exist as a separate entity; rather, it is only when situated within an aggregate that it is subject to transformation. In that case, however, past and future matter would not be considered matter.
That too is matter (*rūpa*)—whether already manifested, about to be manifested, or of that same nature—just like fuel.
In that case, does it follow that non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) is not matter? It is indeed matter.
It is not so, because there is no modification, unlike the movement of a shadow when a tree moves.
Furthermore, upon the cessation of informative action (*vijñapti*), non-informative action (*avijñapti*) would also cease, just as there is no shadow when a tree is absent.
Others say that it is because its basis (*āśraya*) consists of matter (*rūpa*).
If that were the case, then visual consciousness and the others would also follow as being matter, since their bases are also matter.
This comparison is inappropriate.
For non-informative matter (avijñapti) exists depending upon the primary elements (bhūta), just as a shadow depends on a tree or light depends on a gem;
however, visual consciousness and the other [sensory consciousnesses] do not exist by depending on the eye and the other [senses] in that same manner.
These [causes] serve merely as the conditions for their arising.
This, however, is not the Vaibhāṣika position, because they maintain that a shadow exists depending on a tree, and a radiance exists depending on a gem,
since they admit that the atoms of color such as shadows each depend upon their own set of four primary elements (*bhūtacatuṣka*).
Moreover, even though shadow and light are dependent upon their respective bases, it is not tenable for non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) to be dependent in the same way;
for it is accepted that non-informative matter does not cease even when its bases, the great elements (*mahābhūta*), have ceased.
Therefore, this is not a valid rebuttal.
Others, however, offer this rebuttal here:
the bases of visual consciousness and the others have become differentiated;
some, such as the eye and so forth, are subject to transformation (*rūpyate*).
The mind is not transformed;
however, non-informative matter (avijñapti) is not like that.
Therefore, the logical consequence is not the same.
Thus, for this reason, it is established that "matter" (rūpa) is so called because of its susceptibility to transformation (rūpaṇa).
Those very faculties and objects whose intrinsic nature as the aggregate of form has been described are intended here as the ten bases and elements.
In the systematic presentation of the bases, they constitute the ten bases:
the eye-base, the form-base, and so on, up to the body-base and the tangible-object-base.
In the classification of the elements (dhātu), those same ten elements are: the eye element, the form element, up to the body element, and the tangible object element.
The aggregate of form has been explained, as well as its arrangement into bases and elements.
Feeling and the other aggregates must now be explained.
Among them, feeling is experience;
the aggregate of feeling consists of three kinds of experience.
It is pleasant, painful, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant.
When further divided, it consists of the six groups of feeling:
feeling born of eye-contact, up to feeling born of mind-contact.
Perception has the nature of grasping signs. (14)
The apprehension of signs such as blue, yellow, long, short, female, male, friend, enemy, pleasure, pain, and so forth, is the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*).
When further divided, it consists of six groups of perception, just like the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā*).
The aggregate of formations, however, consists of those other than the four;
that is, the formations other than the four—form, sensation, perception, and consciousness—are the aggregate of formations.
However, the Blessed One stated in the Sūtra, "There are six groups of volition," because of its preeminence;
for since it is the very nature of karma, it is primary in the act of formative construction (*abhisaṃskaraṇa*).
Therefore, the Blessed One said: "It constructs the conditioned."
Therefore, it is called the aggregate of the appropriation of formations (*saṃskāropādānaskandha*).

Otherwise, because the remaining mental factors (*caitasika*) and the dissociated factors (*viprayukta*) would not be included within the aggregates, they would not constitute the truths of suffering and its origin; consequently, there would be no full comprehension (*parijñā*) or abandonment (*prahāṇa*) of them.
And it was said by the Blessed One: "I do not say that the end of suffering can be achieved without having directly known and fully comprehended even a single dharma."
Thus it has been said, "without abandoning.
Therefore, it must necessarily be admitted that these are included within the aggregate of formations (saṃskāraskandha).

Furthermore, these three—the aggregates of feeling, perception, and mental formations—are designated as the sphere of phenomena (dharmāyatana) and the element of phenomena (dharmadhātu) in the classification of spheres and elements, together with non-informative matter (avijñapti) and the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta). //15//
Thus, these seven substances are designated as the sphere of phenomena (dharmāyatana) and the constituent of phenomena (dharmadhātu).
Consciousness is individual representation.
The representation and apprehension of each respective object is called the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*).
Furthermore, it consists of the six groups of consciousness.
From visual consciousness up to mental consciousness—
this which has been called the aggregate of consciousness (vijñānaskandha) is, in the systematic arrangement of the bases (āyatana), the mind-base (manāyatana).
In the systematic arrangement of the elements (dhātu), that same [aggregate] is considered to be seven elements.
Which seven?
The six consciousnesses and, moreover, the mind. //16//
The eye-consciousness element up to the mind-consciousness element, and the mind element.
Thus, herein the five aggregates, the twelve bases, and the eighteen elements have been explained.
The aggregate of form (rūpaskandha), excluding unmanifest form (avijñapti), consists of ten bases (āyatana) and ten elements (dhātu).

The three aggregates beginning with sensation (vedanā), unmanifest form, and the unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta) constitute the base of mental objects (dharmāyatana) and the element of mental objects (dharmadhātu).
The aggregate of consciousness (vijñānaskandha) consists of the mind base (manāyatana), the six consciousness elements (vijñānadhātu), and the mind element (manodhātu).
But has it not been stated that the aggregate of consciousness consists of the six groups of consciousness?
Then what is this mind-element (*manodhātu*) that is distinct from them?
Indeed, there is nothing else at all.
What then? That very consciousness among those six which has just passed away is the mind (*manas*).
Whatever consciousness has ceased in immediate succession is called the mind-element (*manodhātu*).
It is just as one says: "That same person who is a son becomes the father of another," or "That same fruit becomes the seed of another."

If that is so, then in terms of substantial entities (*dravyataḥ*), there would be seventeen elements—or twelve—because of the mutual inclusion of the six consciousness-elements and the mind-element. Why, then, are eighteen established?
Even though this is the case, the elements are traditionally taught as eighteen for the sake of establishing a basis for the sixth [consciousness]. (17)
The five bases, such as the eye-element and its corresponding sense-field, serve as the supports for the five consciousness-elements.
Since there is no other support for the sixth, the mind-consciousness-element,
the mind-element (*manodhātu*) was taught in order to establish its support.
Thus, by way of establishing the sixfold sets of basis, based, and object, there are eighteen elements (dhātus).
In that case, the final mind of an Arhat would not be the *manas*,
for there exists no [subsequent] mind for which it would be the immediately preceding past condition (*samanantarātīta*).
No;
for that too exists in the form of the mind.
However, due to the deficiency of other causes, there is no arising of a subsequent consciousness.
In this regard, all conditioned phenomena are subsumed under the aggregates (*skandha*);

all contaminated phenomena are subsumed under the aggregates of clinging (*upādānaskandha*); and all dharmas are subsumed under the bases (*āyatana*) and elements (*dhātu*). However, it should be understood that, in brief, the subsumption of everything is achieved by means of a single aggregate and a single base.
And by means of the element:
it should be understood that all phenomena are subsumed by the aggregate of form, the sense-base of mind, and the element of phenomena.
Indeed, wherever this subsumption is mentioned, it should be understood as being by way of intrinsic nature.
Not by way of another's nature.
What is the reason? Because of being devoid of another's nature. //18//
For a phenomenon is indeed dissociated from that which is other than itself;
therefore, it is not logical that it should be subsumed by that very thing from which it is dissociated.

For example, the visual faculty is subsumed by the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), by the sense-field (*āyatana*) and element (*dhātu*) of the eye, and by the truths of suffering and its origin (*duḥkha-samudaya-satya*).
Because it has that as its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*);
it is not [included] by other aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth, because it is devoid of their intrinsic nature.

As for the inclusion of one thing by another—such as the inclusion of assemblies by the means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*)—that should be understood as merely conventional (*sāṃketika*), since it occurs only occasionally.
But surely there ought to be twenty-one elements,
because of the duality of the eyes, and likewise of the ears and the nose?
It need not be so.
Because of the commonality of genus, object, and consciousness, the eyes and so forth constitute a single element (*dhātu*) even though they are twofold.
Among these, the commonality of genus exists because both possess the intrinsic nature of the eye.
There is a commonality of objective domain because both have visible form as their object;
there is a commonality of consciousness because both have the same eye-consciousness as their support.
Therefore, the eye-element is indeed one.
The same should be applied to the ear and the nose as well.
But the arising of the pair is for the sake of beauty. //19//
Nevertheless, although the eyes and so forth belong to a single element, the occurrence of two of each is for the sake of the beauty of the physical basis;
otherwise, there would be great deformity due to the occurrence of only one location for the eye and ear, and a single nostril.
The aggregates, bases, and elements have been explained.
However, this must be stated: what is the meaning of "aggregate" (*skandha*), "base" (*āyatana*), and "element" (*dhātu*)?
Aggregates, bases, and elements have the meanings of "heap," "gate of arrival," and "lineage," respectively.

From the statement in the Sūtra: "Whatever form there is—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—all that, having been gathered together into one, is designated as the 'form aggregate' (*rūpaskandha*)," it is established that the meaning of "aggregate" is "heap."
Therein, past form is ceased by impermanence;
future [form] is unarisen;
present [form] is arisen but not yet ceased.
The internal is that which belongs to one's own continuum;
the external is other than that.
Alternatively, they are distinguished by way of the sense bases (*āyatana*).
The gross is with resistance;
the subtle is without resistance;
or they are relative.
If it is argued that [the argument] is unestablished because of its relativity,
we say no;
for there is a difference in what is being related to.
That which is coarse in relation to something is never subtle in relation to that same thing, as in the case of a father and a son.
That which is inferior is afflicted;
that which is sublime is unafflicted.
The distant is the past and the future;
the near is the present.
This applies likewise up to consciousness.
But this is the distinction:
the gross [consciousness] has the five sense-faculties as its basis;
the subtle [consciousness] is mental.
"Or by way of the stages," say the Vaibhāṣikas.
The Venerable One said: "Gross form is that which is apprehended by the five sense-faculties;
subtle is the other.
Inferior is that which is unpleasant."
Exquisite and pleasing;
distant and in a place beyond sight; near and in a place within sight.
Because the past and so forth are denoted by their own respective terms, they [the dharmas] are to be understood [as such];
however, their distance or proximity is due to the influence of their bases (āśraya).
"Coarseness and subtlety, however, are as previously described. Thus [it is said].

The meaning of "base" (*āyatana*) is the sense-gate through which mind and mental factors arise. As for its etymological derivation: they are called bases because they extend (*tanvanti*) the arrival (*āya*) of mind and mental factors; that is to say, they expand them.
The meaning of *gotra* is the meaning of *dhātu*.

Just as in a single mountain many *gotras*—such as iron, copper, silver, gold, and so forth—are called *dhātus*, so too, within a single basis (*āśraya*) or continuum (*saṃtāna*), eighteen *gotras* are called the eighteen *dhātus*.
In this context, "mines" (*ākara*) are what are called *gotras*.
Of what are these— the eye and the others— the causes? They are the causes of their own kind, because they function as homogeneous causes (*sabhāga-hetu*).
In that case, the unconditioned would not be a *dhātu*.
[Objection: Then it must be for the mind and mental factors.
[Response: Others say that this word *dhātu* denotes a genus (*jāti*).
The eighteen types of phenomena, which are their intrinsic natures, are the eighteen elements (dhātus).
If the meaning of "aggregate" (skandha) were the same as the meaning of "heap" (rāśi), it would follow that the aggregates are merely nominally existent (prajñaptisat),
because they are collections of multiple substances, like a heap or a person (pudgala).
This is not so.

Because even a single substantial atom (dravyaparamāṇu) is a "aggregate" (skandha), it should not be said that the meaning of "aggregate" is the sense of a "heap. For a single entity does not possess the nature of a heap.
Others maintain that the meaning of "aggregate" (*skandha*) is the bearing of the burden of what is to be done, or alternatively, the sense of "division.
For instance, speakers say, "We shall give the gift in three installments."
This [position] deviates from the Sūtra; for the Sūtra speaks only of the meaning of "aggregate" (*rāśi*), stating in detail:
"Whatever form there is—past, future, or present," and so forth.
In that context, it is made known that each instance of past and other forms possesses the nature of an aggregate (*skandha*);
that is, all this—past and other forms—is individually the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).
It is not possible to understand it in such a way.
Because of the statement, "having condensed all that together into one," the aggregates (*skandha*) are therefore merely nominally existent (*prajñaptisat*), just like a heap. [Objection:

In that case, it follows that even the material sense-bases (*āyatana*), such as the eye, would be merely nominally existent, since they consist of many atoms (*paramāṇu*) of the eye and so forth. [Response: No.

Because they are the cause for [the cognition] of all [atoms] taken together, or because they act as the cooperative condition for the object, the sense organ would not be a separate base (*āyatana*).
However, it is stated in the *Vibhāṣā*:
"If one says that an atom is a portion of one element (*dhātu*), one base (*āyatana*), and one aggregate (*skandha*)."
Now, if one does not take [the others] into account,

it is "one element, one base, one aggregate. For indeed, even in the case of a part, there is a metaphorical designation (upacāra) as if it were the whole, just as when one part of a cloth is burned, one says, "The cloth is burned."
For what purpose does the Blessed One undertake the threefold teaching by way of the aggregates and so forth?
He says:
"Because of the threefold nature of the delusions, faculties, and inclinations of those to be trained, there are the three teachings beginning with the aggregates. (20)
"Threefold" means of three types.
It is said that the delusion of sentient beings is of three kinds:
some are deluded regarding mental factors because they grasp at them as a unified self.
Some [are associated] with form alone; some with both form and mind;
the faculties are also of three kinds.
Because their faculties are sharp, middling, or dull,
their inclinations are also threefold;
because they have an inclination for concise, middling, or extensive texts.
For them, respectively, there are three teachings: the aggregates (skandha), the bases (āyatana), and the elements (dhātu).
Thus it is said.

But feeling and perception are established as separate aggregates; thus it is said: "Because they are the root of dispute and the cause of saṃsāra, and for the sake of the order [of the aggregates], feeling and perception are placed as separate aggregates apart from the other mental factors. (21)
There are two roots of dispute:
attachment to sensual desires and attachment to views.
Of these two, feeling and perception are, respectively, the primary causes.

For it is through the power of relishing feeling that one clings to sensual pleasures, and through the power of perverted perception that one holds [wrong] views; these two are thus the primary causes of saṃsāra. For one who is greedy for feeling and possesses perverted perception wanders in saṃsāra.

Furthermore, from the reason for the sequence of the aggregates that will be taught, one should understand that these two are established as separate aggregates even on account of that sequential reason;
and we shall establish this very point in that same context.
Now, why is the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) mentioned among the elements (*dhātu*) and the bases (*āyatana*), but not among the aggregates (*skandha*)?
The unconditioned is not mentioned among the aggregates because it does not fit their meaning.
For if it were mentioned among the aggregates, it could not be included within any of them.
Because it is logically inconsistent;
for that is neither form (*rūpa*) nor even consciousness (*vijñāna*),
and yet it cannot be called a sixth aggregate (*skandha*).
Why?
Because the meaning is untenable;
for it has been stated that the meaning of "aggregate" (skandha) is the sense of a "heap" (rāśi).

Furthermore, the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is not differentiated by distinctions such as past and so forth in the manner that form (*rūpa*) and the other aggregates are; therefore, it could not be designated as the "unconditioned aggregate" (*asaṃskṛtaskandha*) by being subsumed into a single category along with all those [conditioned phenomena].

Indeed, the term "appropriation-aggregate" (*upādānaskandha*) is used for the purpose of making known the basis of affliction (*saṃkleśa*), while the term "aggregate" (*skandha*) is used for the purpose of making known the bases of both affliction and purification (*vyavadāna*).
Since the unconditioned is neither of these two, it is not established among them due to the lack of logical consistency.
Others maintain that just as the cessation of a pot is not the pot itself, so too the cessation of the aggregates cannot be the aggregates.
For them, this same consequence would apply to the elements and the sense-fields as well.
Thus has another classification of the aggregates been explained.
Furthermore, the sequence [of the aggregates] is according to their coarseness, their nature as afflictions, their analogy to a vessel and so forth, and their order of elements. (22)
For form (rūpa) is the most gross of all because it possesses resistance;
among the formless [aggregates], feeling (vedanā) is gross by way of its manifest activity, for people designate it thus: "I have a feeling in my hand," or "I have a feeling in my foot."
Therefore, that which is more important was stated first.
Alternatively, in this beginningless saṃsāra, women and men [act] due to the afflictions, out of greed for sensual gratification.
And the mind is defiled by that; thus, the sequence follows the order of defilement.
Alternatively, it is according to the sense of being like a vessel and so forth;
for the aggregates begin with form.
Or from the perspective of the realms (*dhātu*):
for the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) is characterized by the forms of the objects of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*),
while the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) are characterized by feeling (*vedanā*).
The peak of existence (bhavāgra) is manifested as mere formations (saṃskāra).

These alone are the stations of consciousness (vijñānasthiti), and consciousness is established within them; thus, the sequence of the aggregates (skandha) is for the purpose of demonstrating the field and the seed.
Therefore, there are exactly five aggregates, neither fewer nor more.

For this very reason, due to the cause of their sequence, sensation (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*) are established as separate aggregates from the formations (*saṃskāra*), because these two are more gross and are the causes for the sequence of affliction; indeed, the sequence of the consciousnesses that have them as their objects follows that very order.
Furthermore, among those six, the first five are mentioned before [the mind] because they have present objects;
the five beginning with the eye are mentioned first because they have present objects.
The mind, however, has an unrestricted object.
Some [of the senses] have present objects; because they consist of derived matter (bhautika), four [senses] [have present objects].
The word "previously" (prāk) carries over [from the previous context].
Furthermore, among the five [faculties], four have been explained previously;
this is because their objects are derived matter (*bhautika*).
However, the object of the body faculty is not fixed.
Sometimes [the sense organs perceive] the primary elements (bhūta), sometimes the derivative matter (bhautika), and sometimes both;
others [perceive them] through a more distant or faster operation.
As for the remainder, it was stated previously that they differ from one another according to their respective operations, whether more distant or faster.
For the eye and the ear have distant objects;
therefore, they were mentioned before the other two.
Between those two as well, the activity of the eye reaches even further.
Even when seeing a river from a distance, one does not hear its sound; therefore, that [the ear] was mentioned first.
However, the nose has no functioning at a distance, nor does the tongue.

Because these two function more rapidly, the nose is mentioned first, since it perceives the odor of food even before it has reached the tongue. Alternatively, the order follows their respective positions [in the body]. //23//
Now, in this body, the seat of the eye is situated at the top;
below that is the seat of the ear;
and below that is the seat of the nose.
Therefore, [the eye] is based on the tongue;
that [tongue] is mostly based on the body;
and the mind, moreover, is based on those very same [elements], yet it does not abide in any location.
Their sequence should be according to their respective positions.

But what is the reason that, among the ten bases included within the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), only one is called the base of form (*rūpāyatana*), and among all things whose nature is phenomena (*dharma*), only one is called the base of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*)? He says: "For the sake of distinction, because of its preeminence, and because it includes many supreme phenomena, one base is called 'form' and one is called 'phenomena. (24)
How is it for the sake of specification?

It is so that it may be understood that each of these ten possesses the status of an *āyatana* individually, by way of being established as object (*viṣaya*) and subject (*viṣayin*), and not collectively.

Furthermore, since the form (*rūpa*) which is not designated by the names "eye" and so forth—being specified by the [terms] "eye" and so on—is to be known as the *rūpāyatana*, no other name is stated for it.
Alternatively, it is because the sense-sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*) is predominant;
for it is "formable" (*rūpyate*) by contact with hands and so forth due to its resistance (*sapratighatva*),
and also because it is demonstrable (*sanidarśanatva*).
Because it is defined as "this is here and that is there," even in common worldly usage, that [visible form] alone is recognized as having such a nature, and not the others. Furthermore,
it is precisely for the sake of specification that only one base, the *dharmāyatana*, is mentioned, and not all of them.
Moreover, since many phenomena (dharmas), such as sensation and so forth, are included herein,
they are designated collectively by the term "dharma.
Furthermore, it is because the supreme phenomenon of nirvana is included here, whereas it is not included in the others.

Others maintain that the single sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*) is established as such because it is gross due to its twentyfold nature, and because it is the object of the three types of vision—the physical eye, the divine eye, and the noble eye of wisdom.

Other aggregates, spheres, and elements are also found designated as such in the Sūtras; should these be understood as being included within these [five aggregates, twelve spheres, and eighteen elements], or are they distinct?
They are included within these very ones and are not distinct.

In that regard, first, as for the eighty thousand aggregates of dharma (dharmaskandha) which the Sage proclaimed: they are either speech or names; thus, their inclusion is within [the aggregate of] form (rūpa) or [the aggregate of] formations (saṃskāra). // 25 //
For those for whom the Buddha’s word has speech as its intrinsic nature, these [dharmaskandhas] are subsumed within the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*);
for those for whom it has name as its intrinsic nature, they are subsumed within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*).
Furthermore, what is the measure of a *dharmaskandha*?
"Some say the measure is that of the treatise.
Some, first of all, say that the measure of this very Abhidharma treatise known as the *Dharmaskandha* is six thousand [verses]. And that is [the extent].

Others, however, say that the discourse on each of the aggregates and so forth constitutes a *dharmaskandha* individually— namely, the discourses on the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), elements (*dhātu*), dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), truths (*satya*), nutriments (*āhāra*), meditations (*dhyāna*), immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), formless attainments (*ārūpya*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), bases of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*), factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika*), supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), knowledge resulting from resolve (*praṇidhijñāna*), absence of strife (*araṇā*), and so forth.
But the aggregate of dharma is described as the antidote to conduct. 26.
Thus, they describe eighty thousand types of conduct among sentient beings, distinguished by the variations in their conduct such as passion, hatred, delusion, and pride;
as an antidote to these, the Blessed One taught eighty thousand aggregates of dharma (*dharmaskandha*).

Just as these eighty thousand aggregates of dharma (dharmaskandha) are established within these very five aggregates, so too should other aggregates, sense-bases, and elements be established accordingly; having considered their specific characteristics, they should be subsumed within those already mentioned. (27)

Furthermore, whatever other aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*) are mentioned in other sūtras, they too should be subsumed within these very aggregates and so forth as already described, after having carefully considered their respective individual characteristics as established in this treatise.

Among them, first, of the five aggregates of morality (*śīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), wisdom (*prajñā*), liberation (*vimukti*), and the knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimuktijñānadarśana*), the aggregate of morality is included within the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*);
the remaining four are included within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*).
Of the ten totalities (*kṛtsnāyatana*), eight, being of the nature of non-attachment (*alobha*), are included in the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*);

however, together with their attendants, they are of the nature of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) and are thus included in both the sphere of mind (*manāyatana*) and the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).
The same applies to the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*).

The two spheres of totality—the sphere of infinite space and the sphere of infinite consciousness—and the four [formless attainments] beginning with the sphere of infinite space have the four aggregates as their intrinsic nature, and thus they are included within the sense-spheres of mind and mental objects (*manodharmāyatana*).

The five bases of liberation, having wisdom as their intrinsic nature, are included within the sense-sphere of mental objects; however, when accompanied by their retinues, they are included within the sense-spheres of sound, mind, and mental objects.
Of the two bases, the non-percipient beings consist of ten bases because of the absence of the bases of odor and taste;
those who have reached the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception consist of the mind base and the mental-object base.
Likewise, in the *Bahudhātuka-sūtra*, sixty-two elements are taught.
Their inclusion should be understood according to their respective applications.

Regarding these six elements that have been mentioned there—the earth element, the water element, the fire element, the air element, the space element, and the consciousness element—the characteristics of two of them have not been stated.
Should one understand that space itself is the space element, and that all consciousness is the consciousness element?
He says: "No."
What, then, is that which is called the space-element (ākāśadhātu)? It is the aperture found in doors, windows, the mouth, the nose, and so forth.
What is to be understood by this term "aperture"?
It is said to be light and darkness.
For a cavity is not perceived as anything other than light and darkness;
therefore, it is said that the space element (ākāśadhātu) should be understood as having light and darkness for its intrinsic nature, and as having night and day for its intrinsic nature.
And that very [element] is called "matter neighboring the non-obstructive" (aghasāmantaka-rūpa).
Agha is indeed form located in the Cita hell, so called because of its extreme destructiveness;
that [first dhyāna] is its vicinity.

Others say: it is called "obscure" (*agha*) because it does not offer resistance (*apratighāta*) to other matter therein, and it is called "adjacent" (*sāmantaka*) because it is contiguous with other matter.
The consciousness element is contaminated consciousness. Why is it not called uncontaminated?
Because these six elements are intended as the bases for rebirth. (28)
For these [elements] serve as the basis from the mind at rebirth-linking up until the mind at death;
however, untainted (anāsrava) phenomena are not like this.

This being so, four of these elements are included within the tangible element (spraṣṭavyadhātu), the fifth within the form element (rūpadhātu), and the sixth within the seven consciousness elements (vijñānadhātu).
Furthermore, among these eighteen elements that have been mentioned, how many are with demonstration (*sanidarśana*) and how many are without demonstration (*anidarśana*)?
Here, only one is with demonstration, namely visible form (*rūpa*).
For it can be demonstrated as being "here" or "there."
It is thus stated that the remaining [elements] are non-demonstrable.
How many are with resistance and how many are without resistance?
Ten are with resistance;
they are the material [elements].
Those ten elements which have been mentioned as being comprised within the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) are characterized by resistance (sapratigha).

Resistance (*pratigha*) means obstruction (*pratighāta*). It is of three kinds: resistance as obstruction, resistance regarding the object-field (*viṣaya*), and resistance regarding the objective support (*ālambana*).

In that context, obstruction by resistance (āvaraṇa-pratighāta) is the prevention of another's arising in one's own location; for example, a hand is obstructed by a hand, or a stone by a stone, and vice versa.
Resistance regarding objects refers to the resistance of the sense faculties, such as the eye, toward their respective objects, such as visible forms.
As it is stated in the *Prajñapti*: "There is an eye that is resisted in water but not on land, such as that of fish."
It exists on land but not in water;
[this is] generally the case for humans.
It exists in both places.
For creatures such as porpoises, frogs, piśācas, and fishermen,
it exists in neither case;
this is excluding these aforementioned forms.
There is an eye that is obstructed at night but not by day,
such as that of bats, owls, and the like;
[there is also one] by day but not at night.
Generally, for humans,
as well as for dogs, jackals, horses, leopards, cats, and so forth, [this occurs] both by night and by day.
"Nor in both [cases];
setting aside these modes.
This is the obstruction of the object-field (*viṣayapratighāta*).
Obstruction with respect to the object refers to the mind and mental factors in relation to their own respective objects.
Furthermore, what is the distinction between the object (*viṣaya*) and the focal point (*ālambana*)?
That in which a [cognition] exercises its activity is its object;
that which is grasped by the mind and mental factors is the focal point.
How much less, then, could that which is operating within its own object or upon its objective support be said to be obstructed?
For it does not proceed beyond that.

Alternatively, "resistance" (pratighāta) here means "obstruction" (nipāta), which is the occurrence [of a thing] within its own objective domain. In this context, the ten [bases] should be understood as having resistance by way of "obstructive resistance," because they mutually obstruct one another.

Regarding those dharmas that are "with resistance" (*sapratigha*) by way of resistance to an object, are they also [resistant] by way of resistance as an obstruction? This constitutes a fourfold logical alternative (*catuṣkoṭika*).

The first alternative consists of the seven mind-elements (*cittadhātu*) and that portion of the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*) which is associated (*saṃprayukta*). The second alternative consists of the five sense objects (*viṣaya*).
The third [category] consists of the five sense-faculties (*pañcendriyāṇi*).
The fourth is a portion of the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*) excluding those factors that are associated (*saṃprayuktaka*).

Those factors which are "with resistance" (*sapratigha*) by way of resistance toward an object (*viṣayapratighāta*) are also [necessarily] "with resistance" by way of resistance toward an objective support (*ālambanapratighāta*).
The subsequent statement:
those which are obstructed by way of the object of cognition (ālambana-pratighāta) are necessarily also obstructed by way of the objective field (viṣaya-pratighāta);
however, there may be those that are obstructed only by way of the objective field and not by way of the object of cognition.
The five faculties.

That wherein the obstruction of the mind seeking to arise can be effected by others is to be known as "with resistance" (sapratigha); by the opposite, it is held to be "without resistance" (apratigha).
Thus says the Venerable Kumāralāta.
Those that are with resistance and those that are without resistance have been explained.
Among these eighteen elements (dhātu), how many are wholesome (kuśala), how many are unwholesome (akuśala), and how many are indeterminate (avyākṛta)?
Eight are indeterminate.
Which eight?
Those ten which were stated to be with resistance are the very same, excluding visible form and sound. (29)
The five faculties and the elements of odor, taste, and tangibility—
these eight are neutral because they cannot be defined as being either wholesome or unwholesome.
Others maintain that they are neutral because they cannot be defined in terms of their maturation (*vipāka*).
In this way, the same consequence would also apply to that which is without outflows (anāsrava).
The others are of three kinds. The other ten elements are wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral.
Among them, the seven mental elements are wholesome when associated with non-greed and the other [wholesome roots].
Those associated with greed and so forth are unwholesome;
others are indeterminate.
The dharma-element is wholesome when it consists of the nature of non-greed and so forth, when it is associated with them, when it is originated by them, and also includes analytical cessation.
That which is associated with and originated from the nature of greed and so forth is unwholesome;
others are indeterminate.
The elements of visible form and sound, when originated by wholesome or unwholesome minds, are themselves wholesome or unwholesome, as they are comprised within bodily and vocal intimation.
The other two are neutral;
thus has the state of being wholesome and so forth been explained.
Among these eighteen elements (dhātu), how many are included in the desire realm (kāmadhātu) and how many are included in the form and formless realms (rūpārūpyadhātu)?
All are included in the desire realm;
"included" means they are not dissociated from it, that is to say, they are bound to the desire realm.
In the realm of form, there are fourteen [elements].
In the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), there are fourteen elements, excluding the elements of odor, taste, olfactory consciousness, and gustatory consciousness. (30)
For there, odor and taste do not exist;
because those two constitute edible food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*), and those who are free from desire for that food are reborn there.
Consequently, olfactory and gustatory consciousnesses also do not exist there.
Because of the absence of an object (*ālambana*).
If that were the case, it would follow that the element of the tangible (*spraṣṭavyadhātu*) is also absent there,
because it consists of edible food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*).
That which does not have the nature of food exists there; this same consequence would apply to odor and taste as well. However, there is no enjoyment of odor and taste without ingestion.
However, there is a purpose for the tangible, because it serves as the basis for the sense faculties, as a support, and as clothing.
Therefore, for those who are free from desire for ingestion, odor and taste are useless there, but not so the tangible.
Others, however, say:
By relying on meditative absorption and attainment (*dhyāna-samāpatti*), forms are seen here and sounds are heard;
furthermore, the body is sustained by a specific type of tangible object accompanied by pliancy (*prasrabdhi*).
Therefore, only these three [objects] are possible upon rebirth in the dhyāna realms, but not odor and taste.
If that were so, it would follow that the sense-faculties of the nose and tongue do not exist, because they would serve no purpose.
But there is a purpose:
for without them, the beauty of the physical basis [the body] would not exist, nor would speech.

If this is the purpose, let there be only the physical basis (adhiṣṭhāna) for the sake of beauty and for the sake of speech; let there be no sense-faculty (indriya). However, it is not possible for there to be a physical basis that lacks a sense-faculty, just as in the case of the physical basis of the male organ.
Its non-existence is logical because it would serve no purpose;
however, the bases of the olfactory and gustatory faculties do have a purpose.
Therefore, it is logical that these exist even without their respective faculties.
The production of the sense faculties occurs even when it serves no purpose,
as in the case of those destined to die in the womb;
while it may indeed be purposeless, it is not without a cause.
And what is the cause for the arising of the sense faculties?
It is a specific karma of one who possesses craving for the sense faculties.
Furthermore, whoever is free from craving for objects is necessarily also free from craving for the sense faculties.
The olfactory and gustatory faculties cannot possibly exist in those who have become free from passion regarding their respective objects.
Why, then, would the male faculty not also fail to be produced?
Because it causes ugliness.
What would not be beautiful for those whose private parts are enclosed in a sheath?
Furthermore, arising does not occur by virtue of some purpose;
rather, it occurs by virtue of a cause. Thus, even that which causes ugliness would indeed arise whenever its cause is present.
In that case, does this not contradict the Sūtra which states, "unimpaired, with their faculties complete"?
There is no contradiction here, for the meaning is that they possess all those faculties that exist in that state; thus, they are "not deficient in their faculties."
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that the male faculty [would also exist] there.
However, they describe it thus:
the olfactory and gustatory faculties indeed exist there, but odors and tastes do not.
For craving operates toward the six sense bases by way of the personal existence (*ātmabhāva*), not by way of the objects;
however, it operates toward the male faculty by way of sexual contact.
Therefore, it is established that fourteen elements belong to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*).
The mind-element, the dharma-element, and the mind-consciousness-element belong to the formless realm (*ārūpyāpta*).

Since those who are free from passion for form are reborn there, the ten elements whose intrinsic nature is form, as well as the five consciousness-elements which have those [form-elements] as their basis and objects, do not exist there.
How many are with outflows (*sāsrava*) and how many are without outflows (*anāsrava*)?

These three—the mind element (*manodhātu*), the phenomena element (*dharmadhātu*), and the mental-consciousness element (*manovijñānadhātu*)—which have been mentioned, are both with and without outflows.
Those that are included within the truth of the path (*mārgasatya*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) are without outflows; others are with outflows.
But the remaining [dharmas] are with outflows (sāsrava). // 31 //
The remaining fifteen elements, however, are exclusively with outflows (sāsrava).

How many are with vitarka and with vicāra? How many are without vitarka and with vicāra only? How many are without vitarka and without vicāra? For the five sensory consciousness-elements (vijñānadhātu) are always associated with both vitarka and vicāra.
For these [first five] are coarse because they are outward-directed;
the word "for" (hi) has the sense of restriction.
The final three are of three kinds.
The final three— the mind element (*manodhātu*), the phenomena element (*dharmadhātu*), and the mind-consciousness element (*manovijñānadhātu*)—

are of three types. Among them, the mind element, the mind-consciousness element, and the associated portion of the phenomena element (excluding *vitarka* and *vicāra*) are accompanied by both initial mental application (*savitarka*) and sustained mental application (*savicāra*) in the desire realm and in the first dhyāna.
In the intermediate dhyāna, there is no vitarka and only vicāra.
From the second dhyāna up to the peak of existence (bhavāgra), there is neither vitarka nor vicāra.
Furthermore, the entire dissociated portion of the dharmadhātu and the vicāra within the intermediate dhyāna are likewise without both vitarka and vicāra.

Applied thought (*vitarka*), however, is always without applied thought and consists of sustained thought (*vicāra*) alone, because of the absence of a second applied thought and because of its association with sustained thought.
In the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and in the first dhyāna, sustained thought is not included within these three types [of mind].
How, then, should it be described?
It is without investigation (*avicāra*) and consists of mere initial inquiry (*vitarka*) alone, because of the absence of a second investigation and because of its association with initial inquiry.
For this very reason it is said:
"On the level that possesses both initial inquiry and investigation, there are four types of phenomena."

Those associated [mental factors] that are devoid of investigation (*vicāra*) and initial inquiry (*vitarka*) possess both initial inquiry and investigation. Initial inquiry itself is without initial inquiry and consists of investigation alone. Those that are dissociated [from mind] are without initial inquiry and without investigation.
Investigation is that which consists of mere applied thought and is devoid of sustained thought.
The remaining [dharmas] are devoid of both. // 32 //
The ten material elements and the remaining [elements] are always without vitarka and without vicāra, because they lack association [with mental factors].
If the five groups of consciousness possess both applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), how can they be said to be "without conceptualization" (*avikalpaka*)?
They are without conceptualization by way of the conceptualizations of investigation (*nirūpaṇa*) and recollection (*anusmaraṇa*).
It is said that there are three kinds of conceptualization.
There are the conceptualizations of intrinsic nature, investigation, and recollection; thus,
these [three] possess the conceptualization of intrinsic nature, but not the other two.

Therefore, they are called "non-conceptual," just as a horse with one leg is called "legless. In this context, conceptualization of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-vikalpa*) is discursive thought (*vitarka*).
That [non-conceptual discernment] will be explained later among the mental factors (*caitta*).
As for the other two, what is their intrinsic nature?
They are, respectively: wisdom (*prajñā*) that is distracted and mental, and mindfulness (*smṛti*) that is entirely mental. (33)
Wisdom associated with the mental consciousness is called "mental";
when it is not in a state of meditative concentration, it is called "distracted.
For that is the conceptualization of investigation (*abhinirūpaṇā-vikalpa*).
All mindfulness, whether concentrated or unconcentrated, is indeed mental; it is the conceptualization of recollection.
How many have an object (*sālambana*) and how many are without an object (*anālambana*)? Seven consciousness elements (*cittadhātu*) have an object.
The seven consciousness elements—the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, mind-consciousness, and mind elements—have an object because they grasp their respective spheres (*viṣaya*).
And half [of the dharma-element] is also [without an object] by its very nature. That which has the nature of a mental factor possesses an object.
It is established that the remaining ten material elements and the portion of the dharma-element that is dissociated [from mind] are without objects.
How many are appropriated and how many are non-appropriated?
Nine are non-appropriated.
Which nine?
Those seven that were stated to have objects, together with half of the eighth, as well as sound—
these nine are non-appropriated:
the seven mind-elements, the dharma-element, and the sound-element.
The other nine are of two kinds. //34//
They are both appropriated (*upātta*) and non-appropriated (*anupātta*).
Among them, the present eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body are appropriated;
those of the past and future are non-appropriated.
The present elements of visible form, odor, taste, and tangibility that are inseparable from the sense faculties are appropriated (*upātta*);

others are non-appropriated (*anupātta*), such as those found in hair, body hair, nails, and teeth—excluding their roots—as well as in feces, urine, saliva, nasal mucus, blood, and so forth. What is the meaning of "appropriated"? It refers to that which is grasped by mind and mental factors as their basis (*adhiṣṭhāna*), because they conform to one another through mutual benefit and injury.
That which is called "sentient" in the world.
How many elements have the nature of primary matter, and how many are derived?
The tangible is of two kinds:
primary matter and derived matter.
In that regard, there are four primary elements (bhūta);
derived matter (bhautika) is sevenfold, beginning with smoothness;
the remaining nine material [factors] are derived matter.
The five sense-faculties and four objects—
these nine elements are exclusively derived matter (bhautika),
as is a portion of the dharma-element.
That which is designated as non-informative (avijñapti) is derived from the primary elements;
the remaining seven mental elements (cittadhātu) and the dharma-element (dharmadhātu), excluding non-informative matter, are neither of these two.
“The ten bases are merely the primary elements,” says the Venerable Buddhadeva.
But that is not so,
because in the Sūtra the fourfold nature of the primary elements is determined by their characteristics, such as solidity and so forth.
And because they are tangible;
for hardness and so forth are not grasped by the eye and the other [faculties], nor are color and so forth grasped by the body-faculty.
And it is said in the Sūtra: "O Bhikṣu, the eye is an internal sense-field, derived from the four great elements, a translucent form, visible and possessing resistance; and so on, up to the body."

“Monk, visible forms are an external sense-sphere; derived from the four great elements, they are material, visible, and possess resistance. Sound, monk, is an external sense-sphere; derived from the four great elements, it is material, invisible, and possesses resistance.
The same applies to odors and tastes.”

“Tangible objects, O Bhikṣu, are an external sense-field (*bāhyam āyatanam*); they consist of the four great elements (*mahābhūtāni*) and that which is derived from the four great elements (*upādāya-rūpam*), being material, invisible, and resistant.
By this, it is clearly demonstrated that because the elements are included only within one part of the sense-field of the tangible, the remainder [of the sense-fields] are not elements.

As for what is stated in the Sūtra, “that which is hard or of a harsh nature in the lump of flesh that is the eye,” this is a teaching concerning the lump of flesh itself, which exists inseparably [from the elements].
"Bhikṣu, this person consists of six elements"— this statement in the *Garbhāvakrānti-sūtra* is for the purpose of demonstrating the fundamental substance of a sentient being.
Furthermore, because of the subsequent mention of the six bases of contact (*sparśāyatana*), and because it would otherwise follow that mental factors (*caitta*) do not exist,
