it is not tenable to maintain that the mind itself is the mental factors.
For it is stated in the Sūtra: "Perception and feeling are mental factors; this phenomenon is dependent upon the mind," and because of the mention of "the mind with lust" and so forth.
Therefore, the elements consist of both the primary elements and their derivatives, as previously stated.
How many are accumulated and how many are non-accumulated? Ten material [elements] are accumulated. (35)
The five sense-faculty elements and the five objects are aggregated,
because they consist of a collection of atoms.

Among the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), what cuts, what is cut; what burns, what is burned; what weighs, and what is weighed? Only the four external elements—designated as visible form, odor, taste, and the tangible—and known by such names as the axe and the wood, both cut and are cut.
What is this phenomenon called "cutting"?
It is the production of a division in a stream of aggregation that arises in connection [with its parts].
The body-faculty and so forth are not cut.
Because even when a limb is severed without remainder, that [organ] does not become twofold; for the sense-faculties do not become divided,
since a severed limb is devoid of sense-faculties.
Nor do they cut [one another],
because they are as transparent as the luster of a jewel.
Just as the four external elements both cut and are cut, so too do they burn and weigh.
That very [consciousness] is what is burned, and that very [consciousness] is what weighs;
it is not the sense faculties, because of their transparency, like the luster of a gem;
nor is it sound, because it is discontinuous.
There is a dispute regarding the two [qualities] of burning and weighing. // 36 //
Some say that those same four elements are both the burner and the weighed; others say that the fire element alone is the burner and heaviness alone is what is weighed.

How many elements (dhātu) are born of maturation (vipākaja)? How many are accumulative (aupacayika)? How many are outflowing (naiṣyandika)? How many are possessed of substance (dravyayukta)? How many are momentary (kṣaṇika)? It is said: five internal [elements] are born of maturation and are accumulative.
First, the five internal elements, beginning with the eye, are both born of maturation and accumulative.
There are no [dharmas] that are outflowing,
because there is no outflow distinct from those [already mentioned].
Among these, "born of maturation" (vipākaja) refers to those produced from the cause of maturation (vipāka-hetu).
It is so called by eliding the middle term, as in the case of "ox-cart" (*goratha*);
or rather, karma that has reached the time of its fruition is called "maturation" (*vipāka*),
because it matures (*vipacyate*).
Therefore, those born from that [maturation] are "born of maturation" (*vipākaja*).
Since the fruit is indeed the process of maturing, it is called "maturation" (*vipāka*).
Alternatively, let there be a metaphorical designation of the fruit with respect to the cause, just as there is a metaphorical designation of the cause with respect to the fruit.
“These six bases of contact are to be understood as ancient karma. Thus [it is said].
Those [dharmas] accumulated by means of food, refinement, sleep, and specific meditative concentrations are "accumulative" (*aupacayika*).
Some say they are also increased by celibacy (*brahmacarya*);
however, that [celibacy] would merely prevent deterioration, not cause accumulation.
The continuity of accumulation acts as a protection for the continuity of maturation, like an outer wall.
Sound is both accumulative and outflowing;
it is not born of maturation.
Sound is not [born of maturation].
What is the reason? Because activity proceeds from effort.

If that is so, then what about that which is stated in the *Prajñapti-śāstra*: “From the thorough cultivation of abstaining from harsh speech, the mark of a Great Man consisting of a Brahma-like voice is produced”?
Some say this is a threefold succession:
for from actions come the elements, and from the elements comes sound.
Others say it is a fivefold succession.

For from actions arise the primary elements born of maturation (*vipākaja*); from those, the accumulative (*aupacayika*) elements; from those, the flow-on (*naiḥṣyandika*) elements; and from those, sound.

If that were so, then bodily sensation (*vedanā*) would also not be considered maturation, since it arises from primary elements born of action—unless, like sound, there were a contradiction with reason.
The eight non-obstructive [elements] are both outflowing and born of maturation. //37//
Which eight?
The seven mind-elements and the dharma-element.
They are outflowing results, produced by the similar and universal causes.
Those born of maturation are produced by the cause of maturation.
Those born of accumulation do not exist for non-obstructive [dharmas], because there is no accumulation of them.
The others are of three kinds. The other four remaining elements— the elements of visible form, taste, odor, and the tangible—
are born of maturation (*vipākaja*), are accumulative (*aupacayika*), and are also of outflow (*naiḥṣyandika*).
One [element] possesses substance (*dravya*).
For the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is a substance because of its essential nature;
and since that exists within the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*), the dharma-element alone is endowed with substance.

The last three are momentary: the mind-element (*manodhātu*), the mental-object-element (*dharmadhātu*), and the mind-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*). These are the last according to the order of recitation.

At the first moment of the untainted state—during the brief duration of the acceptance of the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*)—they exist for a single moment as non-outflowing (*anaiḥṣyandika*); therefore, they are called "momentary."
There is no conditioned phenomenon produced by something else that is not a result of outflow (*naiḥṣyandika*).

In this context, the mind associated with the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*) is the mind-element (*manodhātu*) and the mental-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*);
the remaining factors co-arising with it are the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*).

This is now investigated: Is one who, being previously unendowed with the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*), attains its possession, also [simultaneously] endowed with the eye-consciousness-element (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*)? Or is one who is endowed with the eye-consciousness-element also endowed with the eye-element?
He said:
There may be the acquisition of the eye-element and the visual consciousness-element separately, as well as together. (38)
First, there may be acquisition of the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*) separately from the eye-consciousness-element (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*):
namely, one who gradually acquires the eye-faculty in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*),
or one who dies in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) and is reborn in the second or higher meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*).
There may be one who possesses the visual consciousness element but not the visual element:
namely, one born in the second or higher dhyānas who is manifesting visual consciousness,
or one who has passed away from there and is being reborn in a lower realm.
There may also be the case where one simultaneously acquires possession of both [the faculties],
such as when one dying from the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) is reborn in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) or in the Brahma-world (*brahmaloka*).
There may also be the case where one does not acquire either.
Setting aside these modes.
One who is endowed with the eye-element is also endowed with the eye-consciousness-element? This is a fourfold alternative (catuṣkoṭika).
The first alternative is one born in the second or higher meditative absorptions (dhyāna) who is not manifesting eye-consciousness.
The second [category] consists of one who has not obtained or has not lost the eye in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
The third consists of one who has obtained and not lost the eye in the desire realm, as well as one born in the first dhyāna or born in the second dhyāna and above, while seeing.
The fourth consists of those set aside from these aforementioned modes.
In this way, the acquisition and possession of the eye-element and the form-element, as well as of the eye-consciousness-element and the form-element, are to be inferred accordingly.
The word "and" (ca) serves to include this related case, as in the phrase "even together with."
How many elements (dhātu) are internal and how many are external?
Twelve are internal.
Which twelve?
Excluding form and the others,
the six consciousnesses and the six bases— these twelve elements are internal;
however, the six objective spheres, beginning with form, are external.
If the self does not exist, how can there be anything internal or external?
Because it is the basis for the notion of "I," the mind is metaphorically designated as the "self.
As it has been said: "For by means of a well-tamed self, the wise person attains heaven."
Furthermore, the Blessed One has spoken of the taming of the mind elsewhere: "The taming of the mind is good; a tamed mind brings happiness.

Therefore, because the eye and the other [senses] are proximate to the mind—which is the self—by virtue of being its support (*āśraya*), they possess an internal nature (*ādhyātmikatva*); whereas form and the other [objects], by virtue of being objective domains (*viṣaya*), possess an external nature.
If this is so, then it follows that the six consciousness-elements (*vijñānadhātu*) would not be internal.
For these [six consciousnesses] do not become the support of the mind (citta) unless they have attained the state of the mental element (manodhātu).
At that time, they remain as they are and do not transcend their defining characteristic (lakṣaṇa).
Otherwise, the mental element would be exclusively past, and not future or present.
Furthermore, eighteen elements (*dhātu*) are accepted as belonging to the three time periods.
If future and present consciousness did not possess the characteristic of the mind-element (*manodhātu*), then the mind-element could not be established even in the past time;
for there is no deviation of a characteristic across the time periods.
How many elements (dhātu) are homogeneous (sabhāga), and how many are partially homogeneous (tatsabhāga)? First of all, that which is designated as the "dharma" element is exclusively homogeneous.

For when a specific object is fixed for a particular consciousness, if that consciousness has arisen with respect to that object, or is destined to arise, then that object is called "homogeneous" (*sabhāga*).
And there is no such thing as a dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) wherein an infinite mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) has not already arisen or will not arise;
for this thought necessarily arises in all noble persons (*āryapudgala*): "All phenomena are without self."
And for that [consciousness], all phenomena—excluding its own nature and its co-existent factors—are the object-condition (*ālambana*).
Furthermore, since that moment of consciousness is itself the object-condition for another moment of consciousness, all phenomena indeed serve as the object-condition for two moments.
Therefore, the dharma-sphere (*dharmadhātu*) is eternally homogeneous (*sabhāga*).
And the remaining [elements] are "partially homogeneous" (*tatsabhāga*).
The word "and" (*ca*) implies that they are also "homogeneous" (*sabhāga*). What is this so-called "partially homogeneous"?
He who does not perform his own duty. // 39 //
What is meant is this: that which performs its own function is "homogeneous" (*sabhāga*).
In this context, the eye by which one has seen, sees, or will see visible forms is called the "homogeneous eye.
The same should be stated for the others up to the mind, according to their respective activity upon their own objects.
According to the Kaśmīris, the "non-participating" (*tatsabhāga*) eye is of four kinds:
that which has ceased, is ceasing, or will cease without having seen visible forms, and that which is of a nature not to arise (*anutpattidharmin*).
According to the Westerners (*pāścātya*), however, it is of five kinds.
That very same [faculty] characterized by non-arising is divided into two types: that which is associated with consciousness and that which is not associated with consciousness.
In this manner, it should be understood up to the body-faculty.
The mind-faculty, however, when characterized by non-arising, is exclusively "of its own kind" (tatsabhāga).
Those forms which one has seen, sees, or will see with the eye are "homogeneous" (sabhāga).
Those that are "partially homogeneous" (tatsabhāga) are of four kinds:
those which have ceased, are ceasing, or will cease without ever having been seen, and those whose nature is not to arise.

In this manner, up to the tangible objects, they should be understood as being "homogeneous" (sabhāga) or "partially homogeneous" (tatsabhāga) according to the functioning of their respective sense faculties.

That which is the homogeneous (*sabhāga*) eye of one person is [the homogeneous eye] of all; likewise for that which is non-homogeneous (*tatsabhāga*). This applies similarly up to the mind (*manas*).
As for visible form (*rūpa*), it is "homogeneous" (*sabhāga*) for one who sees it, and "non-homogeneous" (*tatsabhāga*) for one who does not see it. What is the reason?
For there is the possibility that a single person sees a certain form while many others may also see it, as in the case of viewing the moon, a dancer, or a wrestler.
But it is impossible for two people to see with a single eye;
therefore, because this [eye] is not shared, its establishment is by way of a single continuum. Form, however, being shared, is established by way of multiple continua.
Just as it is with the element of form, so should the elements of sound, odor, taste, and the tangible be understood.
Let it be so for sound.

However, as for odors and the rest, those which are perceived by one [sense] are not perceived by another, because they are perceived through contact; thus, due to their specific nature, it is logical to extend the same principle to them as to the eye and the other [senses].
This is indeed so.
However, even these [objects] possess commonality with respect to their arising;
for it is possible that the very same odors and so forth which produce olfactory consciousness and the rest for one person would likewise produce them for others.
But this is not the case for the eyes and the other sense organs.
Therefore, their extension [of properties] is exactly like that of form and the other [sensory objects].
The visual consciousnesses and so forth possess the state of being homogeneous or partially homogeneous because they have the nature of either arising or not arising, just like the mind-element.
What is the meaning of "homogeneous" (*sabhāga*)?
"Part" (*bhāga*) refers to the mutual sharing among the sense faculty, the object, and consciousness, or the sharing of their activity.
That which possesses this [part] is "homogeneous."
Or, it is because they have the same effect as contact (*sparśa*).

Furthermore, those which are non-homogeneous (*asabhāga*) are called "partially homogeneous" (*tatsabhāga*) because they are homogeneous with those [elements] that are homogeneous (*sabhāga*) by virtue of their commonality of genus (*jātisāmānya*).

How many elements (dhātu) are to be abandoned by seeing (darśanaheya), how many are to be abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanāheya), and how many are not to be abandoned (aheya)? First, the ten material elements and the five consciousness-elements are to be abandoned by cultivation.
The last three are of three kinds:
the mind element (*manodhātu*), the mental-object element (*dharmadhātu*), and the mind-consciousness element (*manovijñānadhātu*).
These three elements, being the final ones in the order of recitation, are of three types.
The eighty-eight latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), along with their co-arising factors, their acquisitions (*prāpti*), and their attendants, are to be abandoned by insight (*darśanaheya*).
The remaining contaminated (*sāsrava*) factors are to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanāheya*).
The uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) factors are not to be abandoned.

But is it not the case that there are other things to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*), such as the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) and the bodily and vocal actions leading to the miserable realms (*āpāyika*), because these are in opposition to the Noble Path? [Response: That is not to be abandoned by insight.
This is the summary:
that which is not afflicted is not to be abandoned by vision, nor is form.
There is nothing whatsoever that is both non-afflicted and to be abandoned by vision, nor is there any such form.

And the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) is undefiled-neutral (*akliṣṭāvyākṛta*), because even those who have severed their roots of virtue (*samucchinnakuśalamūla*) or those who are free from passion (*vītarāga*) still possess it.
Form (*rūpa*) consists of bodily and vocal action;
therefore, it is not to be abandoned by insight (*darśanaprahātavya*).

Because there would be no misconception regarding the truths, and because it would follow that one would still be an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) during the receptivity to the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*); nor is it born from a non-sixth [sense-organ]. (40)
The sixth is said to be the mind-base (*manāyatana*).

Therefore, that which arises other than from that [sixth base], namely what is "not born from the sixth" (*aṣaṣṭhaja*) and what is born from the five sense-faculties, is also not to be abandoned by seeing (*darśanaprahātavya*).
Among the eighteen elements (dhātu), how many are views (dṛṣṭi) and how many are not views?
The eye and a portion of the element of phenomena (dharmadhātu) are views.
To the question "Which is that [portion]?", he says:
It is eightfold:

the five views beginning with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), mundane right view, the view of one in training (*śaikṣī dṛṣṭi*), and the view of one beyond training (*aśaikṣī dṛṣṭi*). This eightfold constituent of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) is "view"; the remainder is not view.
Among these, the explanation of the view of a self-identity and the others will be given at the appropriate time in the exposition of the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).
Furthermore, mundane right view is wholesome, contaminated wisdom associated with the mental consciousness;
the uncontaminated view of one in training is that of a trainee;
and that of one beyond training is that of one beyond training.
The vision of phenomena through defiled, undefiled, mundane, trainee, and non-trainee views is like seeing forms on a cloudy night or a cloudless day.

Now, why is it said that mundane right view is associated only with the mental consciousness? Because wisdom arising simultaneously with the five sensory consciousnesses is not "view," as it lacks the capacity for judgment (*atīraṇāt*). (41)
For a view (*dṛṣṭi*) is investigative because it functions through close examination;
however, the wisdom (*prajñā*) co-arising with the five consciousnesses is not like this.
Therefore, that [wisdom] is not a view.
For this very reason, no other wisdom—whether afflicted or non-afflicted—is considered "view."
Now, if the eye does not possess the capacity for investigation, how can it be "vision"?
It is so called in the sense of the observation of form,
because the eye sees forms.
If the eye were to see, then even one who possesses another consciousness would see; however, it is not the case that every eye sees. What then? Only that which is "functioning" (sabhāga) sees.
When it is accompanied by consciousness, then it sees; at other times, it does not.
If that is so, then let it be that the consciousness itself, supported by the eye, sees.
It is not [the eye] that is supported by it.
It can be determined that consciousness sees.
What is the reason?
For a form that is obstructed is indeed not seen. // 42 //
For it is said that form obstructed by walls and the like is not seen.
If consciousness were to see, then because it is non-obstructive, there would be no resistance against walls and such; thus, one should see even obstructed form.
However, visual consciousness does not arise with respect to what is obstructed; how then could that which has not arisen see?
What, indeed, does not arise?

For one who holds that the eye sees, since the eye possesses resistance (*sapratighatva*), there is an absence of its activity toward what is obstructed; thus, it is logical that consciousness also does not arise, because it functions with respect to the same object as its basis (*āśraya*).
But is the eye actually in contact with its object, like the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*), such that it would not see what is covered due to its resistance?
How is it that what is screened by glass, mica, crystal, or water is seen?
Therefore, it is not because of the eye's resistance (*sapratighatva*) that a covered form is not perceived.
What then?
Where there is no obstruction of light, even when a form is concealed, visual consciousness certainly arises;
but where there is an obstruction, it does not arise. Thus, because it has not arisen, one does not see what is concealed.

As for what is stated in the Sūtra, "having seen forms with the eye," the intended meaning here is "by means of that basis," just as one says, "having cognized phenomena with the mind. And yet, the mind does not cognize phenomena [at that moment], because it has already passed away.
What then? It is the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Or rather, the action of that which is supported is metaphorically attributed to the support, just as one says, "The beds are crying out."
Furthermore, as it is said in the Sūtra: “Forms cognizable by the eye are desirable and lovely.
Yet these forms are not cognized by the eye itself.
And it is said in the Sūtra: “The eye, O Brahmin, is merely a gateway for the seeing of forms. From this it is understood that consciousness sees by means of the eye as its gateway.
In that context, the term "vision" (darśana) refers to the door;
for it is not logical [to say], "the eye is vision for the seeing of forms."
If consciousness sees, then who is it that cognizes? And what is the distinction between these two?
For that which is the cognition of a form is itself its seeing.
Just as a certain wisdom is said both to "see" and to "cognize," so too a certain consciousness is said both to "see" and to "cognize."
Others, however, say:

"If the eye sees, one must state what other act of seeing there is for the eye which has become the agent"; [they argue that] in this case as well, there would be a distinction between the agent and the action.
Others, however, say: visual consciousness is the seeing; because it is the basis for that [seeing], the eye is said to "see," just as a bell is said to "ring" because it is the basis for the sound.
But if this is so, does it not follow that the eye perceives because it serves as the basis for consciousness?
It does not follow;
for in common worldly usage, it is that consciousness which is conventionally designated as "seeing."
For when that [eye] has arisen, it is said that "form is seen," not that it is "cognized.
It is also stated in the *Vibhāṣā*: "That which has reached the eye and has been experienced by visual consciousness is called 'seen'.
Therefore, it is only said that "the eye sees," not that it "cognizes."
Consciousness, however, is said to cognize form by its mere presence,
just as the sun is called the "maker of the day."
On this point, the Sautrāntikas say:
"Why is this space being gnawed at?
For it is in dependence upon the eye and visible forms that visual consciousness arises."
In this regard, who sees or what is seen?
For this is devoid of activity, being merely phenomena and merely cause and effect.
Therein, for the sake of conventional usage, metaphorical designations are made at will, such as "the eye sees" or "consciousness cognizes."
One should not be dogmatically attached to this;
for it was said by the Blessed One: "One should not be dogmatically attached to local dialects, nor should one pursue the common designations of the world."
This, however, is the established tenet (*siddhānta*) of the Vaibhāṣikas of Kaśmīra:
"The eye sees, the ear hears, the nose smells, the tongue tastes, the body touches, and the mind cognizes."
Now, if the eye sees, does it see forms with one eye or with both? There is no fixed rule here;
it sees with both eyes as well, because the vision is clearer.
The Abhidharmikas maintain that one sees with both eyes as well;
for when both are open, the vision is more perfectly clear.
Moreover, when one eye is opened and the second is half-closed, there occurs the perception of two moons and so forth.
It is not due to the alteration of one or the other,
nor does it follow that consciousness is subject to interruption through the separation of its basis, because— unlike material form— it is not localized in space.
If the eye sees, the ear hears, and so on up to the mind cognizing, do these [faculties] reach their objects or not?
The eye, ear, and mind have non-reached objects.
For instance, one sees a form from afar, yet does not see the collyrium applied to the eye itself.
One hears sound from a distance.
Furthermore, if [the sense organs] function by reaching their objects, then the divine eye and ear would not arise here for those practicing meditation, just like the nose and other [senses].
If the eye perceives its object without reaching it, why does it not see everything that is not reached—namely, what is distant or obstructed?
First of all, why does a magnet not attract all iron that has not yet reached it?
And even if its object were something reached, this [objection] would be the same:
why does it not see everything that has been reached, such as collyrium or an applicator-stick?

Just as the objects of the nose and other [senses] are those with which they come into contact, yet not all [objects are grasped]—precisely because they do not grasp co-existent odors and so forth—likewise, for the eye, [the object] would be non-contacted, yet not all [non-contacted objects are grasped].
But the mind, being formless, is incapable of coming into contact at all.
Some, however, consider the ear to have both contacted and non-contacted objects.
Because sound is heard even within the interior of the ear.
But the remaining three, known as the nose, tongue, and body, are otherwise. (43)
The meaning is "having reached its object.
How is the sense of smell one that has reached its object? Because there is no perception of odor for one who is not breathing.
What is this so-called "attainment"?
It is arising without interval.
Furthermore, do atoms touch one another or not?
The Kashmiris maintain that they do not touch.
What is the reason?
If they were to touch with their entire substance, the entities would become intermingled; if they were to touch with only one part, it would follow that they possess parts,
yet atoms are partless.
How, then, does the production of sound occur?
Precisely for this reason;
for if they were to touch, a hand struck against a hand would stick to it, and a stone against a stone.
How is it that what has been accumulated does not disintegrate when struck?
Because it is sustained by the wind element (*vāyudhātu*).
Some wind elements function to scatter, as during the period of destruction (*saṃvartanī*); some function to sustain, as during the period of evolution (*vivartanī*).
How, then, is it said that the triad [of sense organs] has reached its object through uninterrupted contact?
Their very state of being "uninterrupted" is simply that there is nothing at all between them.
Furthermore, since aggregates possess parts, they do indeed touch; thus, there is no fault.

And by taking it in this way, this passage in the *Vibhāṣā* also becomes logical: having asked, "Does that which is touched arise from a cause that is touched, or rather from a cause that is not touched? it says: "With respect to the cause, sometimes that which is not touched arises from a cause that is touched, as when it disintegrates;
sometimes that which is touched arises from a cause that is not touched, as when it undergoes accumulation;
and sometimes that which is touched arises from a cause that is touched, as when there is the accumulation of things already accumulated."
"Sometimes [an object] is unperceived even though its cause has been perceived, as for example, dust motes in a window beam. Thus [it is said].
"If atoms were to touch one another, they would persist into the subsequent moment," says the Venerable Vasumitra.
"They do not touch;
rather, the designation 'touching' applies when there is no interval between them," says the Venerable [Dharmatrāta].
And the opinion of the Venerable [Vasumitra] must be accepted;
otherwise, what would obstruct the movement of atoms that have intervals between them through those empty spaces, given that they are held to be characterized by resistance?
Furthermore, aggregates are not something other than the atoms themselves.
It is those very aggregates that are touched, just as they are perceived through their form.

Furthermore, if a distinction of spatial parts is imagined for the atom, then whether it is touched or untouched, the consequence follows that it must possess constituent parts; if no such distinction is imagined, then even for that which is touched, the aforementioned consequence does not arise.

Furthermore, do these [faculties], beginning with the eye, grasp an object equal in dimension to themselves—such that mountains and the like appear as such due to rapid succession, like a whirling firebrand—or do they grasp objects both equal and unequal?
Regarding those which were stated to reach their objects, it is held that by these three beginning with the nose, there is the grasping of an object equal [in size].
For as many atoms as there are in the sense-faculty, so many atoms of the object come together to produce consciousness.
Regarding the eye and the ear, however, there is no fixed rule:
sometimes they perceive fewer [atoms], as when one sees the tip of a hair; sometimes they perceive an equal number, as when one sees a grape.
Sometimes it is larger when one perceives a great mountain with a mere opening of the eyes;
in the same way, this should also be applied to the hearing of sounds such as mosquitoes or thunderclouds by means of the ear.
As for the mind, however, since it is indeed formless, no determination of its size is considered.
Furthermore, what is the arrangement of these atoms of the sense-faculties, such as the eye?
First, the atoms of the visual faculty are situated within the pupil of the eye like cumin flowers;
however, being covered by a transparent membrane, they do not scatter.
Others maintain that they are situated like a mass (piṇḍa) in a vertical and horizontal arrangement;
yet they do not obstruct one another because they are transparent like crystal.
The atoms of the auditory faculty are situated within the interior of the ear-canal (bhūrja).
The atoms of the olfactory faculty are like a bundle of sticks within a jar;
the first three faculties are situated like a garland;
the atoms of the gustatory faculty are like a half-moon.
It is said that [the faculty] occupies only the size of a hair-tip in the middle of the tongue, being not pervaded by the atoms of the tongue-faculty;
the atoms of the body-faculty are situated like the body itself;
and the atoms of the female-faculty are like the hollow of a drum.
The atoms of the male faculty are like a thumb.
In that regard, the atoms of the eye-faculty are sometimes all functioning (sabhāga), sometimes non-functioning (tatsabhāga), and sometimes some are functioning while others are non-functioning;
this remains the case up to the atoms of the tongue-faculty.
However, not all atoms of the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) are "homogeneous" (*sabhāga*).
For even among those confined within the blazing hells, immeasurable atoms of the body-faculty are "non-homogeneous" (*tatsabhāga*).
It is said that if consciousness were to arise through all [atoms] together, the physical basis (*āśraya*) would disintegrate.

Neither a single sensory atom (*indriya-paramāṇu*) nor a single object atom (*viṣaya-paramāṇu*) produces consciousness, because the five groups of consciousness have as their basis and their object that which is accumulated (*saṃcita*). For this very reason, the atom is non-demonstrable (*anidarśana*), since it is invisible. Regarding these six elements of consciousness (*vijñāna-dhātu*) mentioned—ranging from eye-consciousness to mind-consciousness—is their basis the same as their object? For the first five, the object is present, whereas for the last one (mind-consciousness), it belongs to all three times; is the case the same for their basis?
"No," he says.
What then? The basis of the last [consciousness] is past.
For the element of mental consciousness (*manovijñānadhātu*), the immediately preceding ceased mind is the basis.
And for the five [faculties], there is also [acquisition] simultaneous with them. // 44 //
The word "and" (*ca*) indicates that they are also past.
In this regard, the eye is the simultaneous support (*sahaja-āśraya*) for visual consciousness, and so on, up to the body being the support for tactile consciousness.
Furthermore, their past support is the mind (*manas*); thus, these five groups of consciousness (*vijñānakāya*) are supported by two types of faculties.
Therefore it is said: "That which is the basis for visual consciousness is also its immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*); this constitutes a fourfold alternative (*catuṣkoṭika*).
The first alternative is the eye;
the second is the mental factors (*caitasika*) of the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*) that have just passed away.
The third [alternative] is the mind that has just passed away;
the fourth category consists of those phenomena excluded from what has been mentioned.
In this same manner, up to the case of body-consciousness, its own respective faculty should be stated.
Regarding mental consciousness,
there is that which is both its basis and its immediately preceding condition; however,
there may also be that which is its immediately preceding condition but not its basis.
The mental factor that has just passed away is the element of phenomena (dharmadhātu).

Furthermore, what is the reason that, although the arising of consciousness depends upon both [the sense organ and the object], only the eye and so forth are called the "bases" (āśraya) and not visible forms and so forth?
The bases are the eye and so forth because they undergo transformation according to the transformation of that [consciousness].
The term "elements" (dhātu) is the governing topic here.

For when there is a change in the eye and so forth, there is a corresponding change in their respective consciousnesses, because they conform to the benefit, injury, acuity, or dullness [of the sense organs].
However, there is no such change in them through a change in visible forms and so forth.
Therefore, because they are dependent upon those [organs], it is the eyes and so forth that are the bases, not visible forms and the rest.
What, then, is the reason that while form and so forth are cognized by them, they are called "eye-consciousness" up to "mind-consciousness," and not "form-consciousness" up to "dharma-consciousness"?
Because these [faculties], such as the eye, are their supports (*āśraya*), and because they are uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*), consciousness is designated by means of them. (45)
How is it that [the eye] is unique?
For the eye is not capable of serving as the support for another consciousness;
whereas visible form, however, serves as the object of mental consciousness as well as of other visual consciousnesses.
In this way, it should be understood up to the body (*kāya*).

Therefore, because they serve as its basis (*āśraya*) and because they are its specific causes (*asādhāraṇatva*), consciousness is designated by them alone and not by visible form (*rūpa*) and so forth;
just as one says "the sound of a drum" or "a barley sprout."

Now, when one situated in a particular body perceives forms with the eye, do that body, eye, form, and visual consciousness belong to the same level (*ekabhūmika*), or can they also belong to different levels?
He replied: there is a distinction among all of them.
For one born in the desire realm who sees their own forms with their own eye, everything belongs to their own level.

For that same person, when seeing their own forms with the eye of the first dhyāna, the body and the forms belong to their own level, while the consciousness and the eye belong to that [first dhyāna] level.
When seeing forms belonging to the level of the first dhyāna, all three belong to that level.

When one sees one's own forms with the eye of the second dhyāna, the body and the forms belong to one's own level (the desire realm), the eye belongs to that level (the second dhyāna), and the consciousness belongs to the level of the first dhyāna.

When seeing the forms belonging to the level of the first dhyāna, the consciousness and the forms belong to that level, the body belongs to the desire realm, and the eye belongs to the level of the second dhyāna.

When seeing the forms belonging to the level of the second dhyāna, the eye and the forms belong to that level, the body belongs to the desire realm, and the consciousness belongs to the level of the first dhyāna.
In the same way, this should be applied to one who, with an eye belonging to the level of the third or fourth dhyāna, sees forms belonging to that level or to lower levels.
For one born in the first dhyāna who sees his own forms with his own eye, everything belongs to his own level; when he sees lower forms, three [factors] belong to his own level.
When he sees his own forms with an eye belonging to the second dhyāna, three [factors] belong to his own level, while the eye belongs to that [second] level.

For one seeing forms belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*), the body and consciousness belong to their own level (*svabhūmika*), the forms are of a lower level, and the eye belongs to that [desire] level.
For one seeing forms belonging to the level of the second dhyāna, the eye and the forms belong to that level, while the remainder belong to their own level.
The same should be applied for the eyes of the third dhyāna and so forth.

For one born in the second dhyāna or higher who sees forms belonging to their own or another level with the eyes of their own or another level, the application should be made accordingly as appropriate.
But this is the fixed rule:
the eye is never of a lower level than the body.
For the body, the eye, and visible forms belong to five levels, ranging from those of the desire realm up to those of the fourth dhyāna.
Eye-consciousness belongs to two levels: that of the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*) and that of the first dhyāna level.
In this regard, the eye belongs to the same level as the body, or it may belong to a higher level, but never to a lower level.
As for the form which is the object, it belongs to the same level as the eye, or it may belong to a lower level.
Form of a higher level is not [perceived] by the eye;
for form belonging to a higher plane can never be seen by an eye belonging to a lower plane.
And the same applies to consciousness.
Above, it is not like the eye with respect to visible form; however, its own form, as well as those of both [eye and ear], exist throughout the entire body. (46)
"For this"—that is, for the visual consciousness just mentioned—visible form (*rūpa*) is the object from all sides: above, below, and on its own level.
For the body, both visible form and consciousness exist from all sides.
Just as this eye has been explained in detail, so too should the ear be understood.
"The ear is not lower than the body, nor is sound higher than the ear;
its consciousness [is not higher than the body], but sound and both [the ear and its consciousness] are in relation to the body everywhere. This should be applied in detail.

However, for the three [elements]—the nose, tongue, and body elements—all are exclusively of their own level (*svabhūmika*). That is, the body, its own object, and its consciousness belong only to their own level.
Having thus established the general rule (*utsarga*), an exception (*apavāda*) is now introduced for the sake of further specification.
Body-consciousness belongs to a lower level or its own level.
The body, the body-element, and the tangible object always belong exclusively to its own level.
However, for some, body-consciousness belongs to its own level, as is the case for those born in the desire realm or the first dhyāna.
For some, it belongs to a lower stage, as in the case of those born in the second dhyāna or above.
The mind is indeterminate. // 47 //
Sometimes the mind belongs to the same level as the body, the mental consciousness, and its objects; sometimes it belongs to a higher or lower level.

For even when the body belongs to one of the five levels, the mind and other faculties can belong to any level at the time of meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) or rebirth (*upapatti*), as the case may be. This will be explained in detail in the section on meditative attainments in the *Kośasthāna*.
However, for the sake of avoiding the burden of excessively voluminous texts, this will not be recounted again now;
for the purpose is small while the labor is great. Thus concludes this incidental discussion.
This is now investigated:
among the eighteen elements (*dhātu*) and the six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*), which is to be cognized by which?
He says:
The five external [elements] are cognizable by two types of consciousness.

The elements of visible form, sound, odor, taste, and tangible objects—having been experienced respectively by the visual, auditory, olfactory, gustatory, and tactile consciousnesses—are subsequently cognized by the mental consciousness.
Thus, each of these is cognizable by two consciousnesses.
It is explained that the remaining thirteen elements (dhātus), because they are not objects of the five groups of consciousness, are to be known by the mental consciousness alone.
Among these eighteen elements, how many are permanent and how many are impermanent?
Not a single element exists in its entirety as permanent.
However, unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) are eternal;
therefore, one part of the dharma-sphere (*dharmadhātu*) is eternal, while the remainder is impermanent.
How many are faculties (indriya) and how many are not faculties?
Half of the dharmas and those which are known as the twelve internal [bases] are faculties. (48)

Twenty-two faculties are taught in the Sūtra: “The eye-faculty, the ear-faculty, the nose-faculty, the tongue-faculty, the body-faculty, the mind-faculty, the female-faculty, the male-faculty, the life-faculty, the pleasure-faculty, the pain-faculty, the joy-faculty, the displeasure-faculty, the equanimity-faculty, the faith-faculty, the energy-faculty, the mindfulness-faculty, the concentration-faculty, the wisdom-faculty, the faculty of ‘I shall come to know the unknown,’ the faculty of ‘knowing,’ and the faculty of ‘one who has known.’”
The Abhidharmikas, however, disregarding the established order of the six sense bases, recite the mind-faculty (*mana-indriya*) immediately after the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*),
because it possesses an object (*sālambanatva*).
In that regard, half of the *dharmas* consists of the eleven faculties beginning with the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) and a portion of the other three, because they are part of the *dharmadhātu*.
Among the twelve internal [faculties], the five beginning with the eye are designated by their own names;
the seven mind-elements (*cittadhātu*) constitute the mind-faculty (*manendriya*).
It will be stated later that the female and male faculties are portions of the body element (*kāyadhātu*).
It is established, therefore, that the remaining five elements and a portion of the mental-object element (*dharmadhātu*) are not faculties.
Thus ends the first treasury-location, titled "Exposition of the Elements," in the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*.
